doc.title: Jonathan Scales interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 23, 2025

title: Saxophone first, then stumbling on the steel pan at Appalachian State
summary: He doubts he would still be in music had he stayed on sax; a friend took him to the panyard at college and the pan felt natural after sax and drumline.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Well that’s deep because with every little thing that happens in life we never know which path takes us down so there’s a chance that if I still played the saxophone, which was my first instrument, maybe I wouldn’t be doing music. There’s no telling, you know? So it’s hard to even make a parallel to say that like I would be doing this except it’d be saxophone. Because I don't know, because like you know the instrument has definitely informed the trajectory of my creativity.
Was there an AHA! moment that sent you to the pans?

It was more like stumbling upon it. So I went to a school in North Carolina called Appalachian State University. And there’s a steel band at the school that’s been there since like 1984 started by Dr. Scott Meister. And when I got to college as a freshman a lot of my friends were trying to pull me in to trying to be in the steel band. They hold open auditions at the beginning of the semester. And you know you learn a couple tunes, they see how you jive with the band, how you vibe with the band, and then that’s how you get into the ensemble. And as an incoming freshman I had no interest in that. Because I was there to study composition, I wanted to be a composer, I’m not trying to join a new ensemble on day one of college. College is big – like I just got here. And a friend of mine was like, “Hey, let me just take you to the panyard.” That’s where they call the rehearsal area. “Let me take you to the panyard so you can just look at it.” So she took me to the panyard and I looked at the pans, and I got to like take a mallet and tap a note. And that’s when I was like this is interesting. And that was just like a moment that kind of like sparked everything.
Nice. Were you struck by the – I didn’t mean to do a little joke there – when you struck it, did the overtones have an impression, make an impression on you?

Not consciously. You know? Maybe there were some subconscious things that I’m not aware of but I think that for me, as a saxophone player – so I went from – I actually went from saxophone to marching percussion, like drumline, when I was a junior and senior in high school. So like I had this melodic sensibility I guess, from saxophone, and then I had like decent hands from doing drumline stuff in high school and being inspired by like DCI and drum corps and that type of, you know that marching experience. So when it came to the pan, when I got to college, it kind of was a natural transition. And I kind of had this natural ability where as soon as I started playing I had a really good sense of it and it felt good to me already even though I’d been playing the saxophone since the sixth grade. It felt better to me, like playing this instrument that I started last week, it just feels more natural to me. So I was able to actually advance further than I ever had on my original instrument. I was never – I never thought I was a good saxophone player.
